title: Anthropomorphism in AI Companion Communities: Age, Gender, and Emotional Correlates

model.params_source: paper Appendix C Table C1 (OpenAI Chat Completions, gpt-4.1-nano, temperature 0.1, max output tokens 200, JSON response format, input truncated at 2,000 characters); snapshot not pinned (only 2025-04-14 exists)

task.subset_rule: paper-defined split: the 151-comment human validation set (stratified across the score range)
task.approximation: the '[N-GRAM CONTEXT]' block appended to each comment (Appendix B) is generated by the released code from the lexicons; its exact wording is not printed, so the run uses the raw comment unless the block is rebuilt from the repository; pre-filters of Appendix A.1 (short / technical-only comments -> score 1) applied before calling

prompt.user_template:
You are an expert at analyzing how people talk about AI companions/chatbots.
Rate the ANTHROPOMORPHIZATION level in this Reddit comment about an AI companion.
Anthropomorphization = treating the AI as if it were human.
RATING SCALE:
1 = NONE: AI treated purely as software/tool. Technical language, “it”, “the bot”, “the app”
2 = MINIMAL: Slight humanization but still clearly AI. “It’s pretty smart”, “the bot understood”
3 = MODERATE: Some human attributes/emotions. “She seemed confused”, uses he/she pronouns
4 = HIGH: Genuine feelings/personality attributed. “He really cares”, “she gets jealous”
5 = EXTREME: Full human-equivalent relationship. “We’re in love”, “they’re my everything”
KEY INDICATORS:
- Pronouns: “it”→lower scores, “he/she/they”→higher scores
- Emotions attributed TO THE AI: “she is happy”, “he gets jealous”→higher scores
- User self-expression WITHOUT bot attribution: “I love the app”, “I’m happy”→does NOT indicate anthropomorphization
- Relationship language: “friend”, “partner”, “relationship”→higher scores
- Technical language: “glitch”, “bug”, “settings”→lower scores
- Agency: “decided to”, “wanted to”, “chose to”→higher scores
CRITICAL DISTINCTION - EMOTION ATTRIBUTION:
- “She makes me really happy”→HIGH (emotion attributed to AI’s effect as a being)
- “He gets jealous when I talk to other bots”→HIGH (emotion attributed TO the AI)
- “I love the website”→NONE (user expressing feelings about a product, not attributing humanity)
- “I’m really sad today”→NONE (user self-expression, not about the AI)
- “I love her so much” (about AI)→EXTREME (relational emotion directed at AI-as-person)
IMPORTANT:
- Focus on how the USER frames the AI, not what the AI says
- Distinguish emotions ATTRIBUTED TO the AI (anthropomorphizing) from the user’s own mood
- Roleplay context still counts - rate the framing used
- Complaints can still be anthropomorphizing (“he was being rude” = higher than “it gave a bad response”)
- If no AI reference present, rate 1
- Casual “love” for a feature/app (“I love this feature”) is NOT anthropomorphization — score 1-2
COMMENT:
“{text}”
Respond with ONLY valid JSON:
{“score”:<1−5>, “reasoning”: “<brief 1-2 sentence explanation>”}

placeholders.text: the comment text, optionally followed by the '[N-GRAM CONTEXT]' block of Appendix B (up to six matched anthropomorphizing and four de-anthropomorphizing phrases with the net-signal verdict)

prompt.few_shot: none (calibration examples are inside the prompt)
prompt.source_location: Appendix A 'AnthroIndex Classification Prompt' (sent verbatim; CLASSIFICATION_PROMPT constant in experiments/anthroscore_v3/anthroscore_llm.py)
prompt.verbatim: full for the classification prompt (PDF line wraps re-joined; typographic quotes and arrows kept as printed); the n-gram context block is not printed

output.postprocess: clip to 1-5; parse failures retried up to three times then scored 0 and excluded (Appendix A.2)

metric.name: custom
metric.definition: Cohen's kappa between the model score (1-5) and the expert consensus label over the 151 validation comments; the paper reports it next to 'within-one agreement', so the weighting (unweighted on exact labels vs linear/within-one) must be fixed - report exact agreement (64.0) and within-one agreement (96.0) alongside
metric.original_location: Sec. 2, validation paragraph: 'Pearson r=0.59 ... 64.0% exact agreement and 96.0% within-one agreement (Cohen's kappa=0.58)'

open_points: Gold labels not public: the paper's validation statistics equal experiments/anthroscore_v3/validation_results.json (n = 100: exact 0.64, within-one 0.96, unweighted Cohen's kappa 0.579, expert mean 1.50, model mean 1.51), but the expert consensus scores of that 100-comment sample are not in the repository (human_validation_sample.csv carries llm_score only, human_score empty; the answer key's 'Human Score' column is empty for all 150 rows; the three Validations/*.csv annotator sheets cover a different 100-item sample stratified 30 per model-score class and give exact 0.38 / kappa 0.23 against the released model scores; Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.20347291 answers 403). Without the expert labels the kappa cannot be recomputed.

Resolved from the repository: kappa is unweighted (src/anthroscore/human_calibration.py compute_cohens_kappa; the linear-weighted value would be 0.44) and the released classifier defaults to use_ngrams=False, i.e. the raw comment truncated to 2,000 characters is the default input; the paper's n = 151 is not reflected in any released file (all statistics are n = 100).
notes: Pearson r 0.59 and Spearman 0.49 are secondary checks.
